headline: Taranaki LNG Terminal Plan Sparks Power-Bill Levy Dispute in Parliament
summary: The Government’s plan to progress an LNG import terminal in Taranaki dominated question time, with ministers forecasting lower power bills and opposition parties questioning how the project will be funded and whether it will deepen reliance on fossil fuels. MPs also debated high unemployment, flood recovery and contested changes to employment law, the Public Service and fiscal reporting; three government bills passed second readings on party-line votes. A veterans-recognition bill advanced with broad support, while debate on financial-market regulation was left unfinished.

topicSummaries.topic: Taranaki LNG Plan Fuels Dispute Over Power-Bill Levy
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The facility’s funding method could affect electricity-sector costs and household bills, while the Government says it will make power more reliable and affordable.
topicSummaries.content: The Government said it would progress an LNG import terminal in Taranaki to provide backup fuel during dry years when hydro generation is under pressure. Energy Minister Simon Watts said a levy on the electricity sector would fund the infrastructure, while the Government’s modelling, as cited by ministers, projected system savings of about $265 million a year, household savings of at least $50 a year, a $1.2 billion annual economic boost by 2035 and protection for about 2,000 jobs. Labour and the Greens challenged the policy’s cost, its impact on household power bills and its reliance on imported fossil fuels; ministers rejected the description of the funding mechanism as a household gas tax. No bill was considered on the announcement.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: So is it a tax, a levy, a fee, a charge—regardless of what he calls it, is it an extra cost every New Zealand household will pay every time they pay their power bill?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: In answer to the first part of the question, absolutely not, because it will lead to lower power bills, not higher power bills.

topicSummaries.topic: Unemployment and Job Losses Drive Economic Debate
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Employment prospects affect household incomes and financial security, particularly for people unable to find work or get enough hours.
topicSummaries.content: Labour MPs cited claims of 32,000 fewer people in work since the Government took office, 165,000 people seeking jobs and 139,000 part-time workers wanting more hours. Finance Minister Nicola Willis pointed to Stats NZ figures showing 15,000 additional jobs in the December quarter, increased hours worked and rising job advertisements, and said economists forecast unemployment would fall as the economy recovered. Labour questioned the Government’s account of the economy, while Willis argued that fast-track projects and other policies would support future job creation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why, then, won’t she take responsibility for the 32,000 fewer jobs compared to when she took office?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our Government has taken responsibility for fixing the economic mess we have inherited, which has involved ensuring that we brought inflation back under control, ensuring that interest rates were supported to drop, and ensuring that firms would be in a better position to create jobs.

topicSummaries.topic: Employment Relations Bill Advances Despite Worker-Rights Opposition
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could affect how gig workers are classified and what protections employees can use if they are dismissed or treated unfairly.
topicSummaries.content: The Employment Relations Amendment Bill passed its second reading by 68 votes to 55, with National, ACT and New Zealand First supporting it and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposing it. Labour MPs argued the bill would make it harder for gig workers to establish employee status, restrict personal grievance claims for some high earners and end the rule that gives new employees initial coverage under a collective agreement. Government MPs said the changes would make the labour market more flexible and rebalance arrangements for employers and employees. The bill proceeds to the next stage of consideration.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Jan Tinetti (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This Employment Relations Amendment Bill doesn’t amend the law, it amputates it.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dan Bidois (National)
keyExchanges.quote: On this side of the House, we believe that the pathway to higher incomes and opportunities is for a more flexible labour market—flexibility for workers in the gig economy, and flexibility for businesses.

topicSummaries.topic: Public Service Bill Passes Second Reading Amid Neutrality Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to public-sector appointments, diversity provisions and long-term advice could affect how government agencies serve the public and maintain independence.
topicSummaries.content: The Public Service Amendment Bill passed its second reading by 68 votes to 55. The Government said it would sharpen agencies’ focus on service delivery, require contestable appointment processes for chief executives, strengthen performance reviews and reduce duplication by replacing agency-by-agency long-term insights briefings with one prepared by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. It also removes specific diversity, equity and inclusion provisions from the Act, which the Government said are covered by other laws. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued the changes risk weakening political neutrality, pay-equity commitments, representation and long-term scrutiny. The bill proceeds to its next stage.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Judith Collins (National)
keyExchanges.quote: These changes are not a politicisation of the Public Service.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Removing the requirement for the Public Service to have a view to the long-term interests of New Zealand means that they are just relegated to managers that implement the desires of Government.

topicSummaries.topic: Fiscal Bill Advances as MPs Clash Over Wellbeing Reporting
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The rules governing fiscal disclosures and budget reporting shape how the public and Parliament assess government spending and its effects.
topicSummaries.content: The Public Finance Amendment Bill passed its second reading by 68 votes to 55. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said it would require more detailed disclosure of fiscal risks, introduce an annual statement on tax concessions and allow alternative fiscal measures within reporting requirements. She argued that the changes responded to gaps in previous disclosures, including temporary funding for Pharmac. Labour disputed that account and said the risks had been signalled; Labour and the Greens also objected to removing statutory wellbeing-reporting requirements, arguing that financial measures alone do not capture effects on health, housing, the environment and other outcomes. The bill proceeds to its next stage.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: By embedding these changes in law, we are taking a proactive step to strengthen fiscal discipline, improve transparency, and build public trust in the Government’s financial management.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Deborah Russell (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The point of the wellbeing Budgets is to try to get a focus on that which makes life worthwhile, and to understand those factors in our country that make life joyful and worth living, and to direct the Government’s attention to them and then to measure Government’s progress towards them.

topicSummaries.topic: East Coast Flood-Affected Communities Seek Recovery Guarantees
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Damage to roads, homes, farmland and community facilities has left some communities isolated and seeking reliable access to schools, hospitals and livelihoods.
topicSummaries.content: During the resumed debate on the Prime Minister’s statement, Labour MP Cushla Tangaere-Manuel described severe flooding in northern Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, where she said a month’s worth of rain fell in 36 hours. She reported damaged roads, homes, schools and community facilities, and said about 30,000 hectares of land, predominantly Māori-owned, had been affected. She called for concrete commitments to reconnect communities and restore access to essential services. The transcript records her appeal but no specific government response during this debate.

topicSummaries.topic: Anzac Day Bill Extends Recognition to More Veterans
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes would broaden who is formally recognised at Anzac commemorations, including people who served in conflicts and roles not covered by the existing law.
topicSummaries.content: The Anzac Day Amendment Bill passed its second reading with support across the House. The 1966 Act lists six wars, while the amendment broadens recognition to cover later deployments, non-military personnel serving in conflict zones and New Zealanders involved in future warlike conflicts. It also updates the Gallipoli reference to include New Zealand and other allied forces. Labour supported the change but raised concerns about access to some veterans’ support, an issue separate from the bill’s recognition provisions.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Jenny Salesa (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: So the thousands of veterans since the parent Act was passed that are not actually recognised or commemorated at Anzac Day is something that we absolutely agree on in the Labour Party that we should look at to ensure that the definition is broadened and that the scope of who and what is commemorated on Anzac Day is indeed recognised.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Damien O’Connor (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: They will go offshore for peacekeeping duties. Those people are serving our country. They are representing us and they are worthy of veteran status, which this piece of legislation will indeed bestow upon them.

topicSummaries.topic: Financial Markets Bill Faces Debate Over Consumer and Climate Rules
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes affect financial firms’ compliance duties and the safeguards available to people buying insurance, borrowing money or using other financial products.
topicSummaries.content: Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Scott Simpson outlined amendments intended to simplify licensing and compliance while retaining consumer protections. The bill would lift the climate-disclosure reporting threshold for listed issuers from $16 million to $1 billion, remove investment scheme managers from the regime and change some liability settings. Labour said it supported several technical changes but warned that reducing conduct requirements could weaken consumer protections, and argued the higher reporting threshold would exclude businesses already reporting. Labour also called for the Financial Markets Authority to have a clearer role in designating buy-now-pay-later products for consumer regulation. Debate was interrupted and is due to resume at the next sitting; no second-reading vote was recorded.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Scott Simpson (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The changes will make it easier for firms to comply with their obligations, strengthen the Financial Markets Authority’s ability to oversee conduct, and, ultimately, improve outcomes for consumers.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This is a bill which swims in the other direction; it makes it easier for institutions—and not all of them, absolutely not, but a few players in the market we’ve seen over time taking advantage of New Zealand consumers because they don’t have some of those protections that other countries we like to compare ourselves to have.

conclusion: The day’s clearest divide was over who bears the costs and risks of government policy—from energy security and employment protections to fiscal accountability and the independence of public institutions.
